questions.stem: Which backup type copies all data, taking the longest to run but allowing the fastest restore from a single set?
questions.explanation: A full backup copies everything. It takes the longest to create, but restore is fast because you only need that one set.
questions.trap: Incremental backups are fast to create but slow to restore - the opposite trade-off from a full backup.

questions.stem: Which backup type backs up everything changed since the original full backup, so restore needs only two sets?
questions.explanation: A differential backs up everything changed since the last full backup. To restore you need just two sets: the full plus the latest differential.
questions.trap: An incremental backs up only changes since the LAST backup of any type, so restore needs the full plus every increment in order.

questions.stem: Which backup type makes daily backups extremely fast but restoration slow and complex because you need the full plus every daily set in order?
questions.explanation: An incremental backs up only the changes since the last backup run, making daily backups fast - but restore is slow because you need the full plus every increment in sequence.
questions.trap: A differential only needs two sets to restore; the incremental's chain of every daily set is what makes its restore slow.

questions.stem: Which backup combines existing full and incremental backups internally to create a new full backup without re-transferring all the data across the network?
questions.explanation: A synthetic full backup merges the existing full and incremental backups internally to produce a brand-new full backup file without re-sending all the data.
questions.trap: A regular full backup would re-transfer everything; the synthetic full avoids that by assembling from what already exists.

questions.stem: Why does the review insist on backup testing?

choices.text: To reduce the storage they consume
To verify the backed-up files are actually readable and restorable
To convert incremental backups into full backups

questions.explanation: Backups are worthless if they don't work, so you perform backup testing to verify the files are readable and can actually be restored.
questions.trap: Testing is about proving recoverability, not about speed or storage savings.

questions.stem: A technician wants to restore files to a separate folder so newer data isn't accidentally overwritten. Which recovery method is this?
questions.explanation: Alternate location recovery restores files to a separate folder, protecting newer data from being destroyed.
questions.trap: In-place recovery overwrites existing files - exactly the risk the technician is trying to avoid here.

questions.stem: In the GFS rotation scheme, what do grandfather, father, and son represent?
questions.trap: GFS describes a time-based rotation, not locations or media types (those belong to the 3-2-1 rule).

questions.stem: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule require?

choices.text: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with at least 1 copy offsite
3 full backups, 2 incrementals, 1 differential each week

questions.explanation: The 3-2-1 rule: keep 3 copies of your data total, on 2 different types of media, with at least 1 copy offsite to survive fire or flood.
questions.trap: The 3-2-1 numbers refer to copies/media/offsite, not to backup types or rotation cadence.

questions.stem: Why does the 3-2-1 rule specifically require at least one copy to be offsite?

choices.text: To protect against a local disaster such as fire or flood
To reduce the number of media types needed

questions.explanation: Keeping at least one copy offsite, far from the building, protects the data against fire, flood, or other local disasters.
questions.trap: The offsite copy is about disaster survival, not speed - and it does not remove the need for testing.

questions.stem: A technician needs the absolute fastest restore after a disaster and is willing to accept slower backup creation. Which single backup type best fits?
questions.explanation: A full backup is slow to create but fast to restore because everything is in one set - ideal when restore speed is the priority.
questions.trap: Incremental backups are the fastest to create but the slowest to restore, the opposite of what's needed here.
